cases.basis: Single-vendor disclosure by the AI provider whose product was abused, with no public IOCs and no independent technical corroboration. The compromise is only visible as an emergent property of the session - tempo, phase progression, target breadth, and the ratio of agent actions to human decisions - which is not something a signature can express. cases.title: SpAIware - Prompt Injection That Persists in Assistant Memory
cases.affects: ChatGPT memory (macOS app) - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Publicly reproducible research by Johann Rehberger with a documented vendor fix, subsequently adopted into the MITRE ATLAS technique set as AI Agent Context Poisoning - Memory (AML.T0080.000).
cases.summary: An injected instruction, delivered through a malicious site or a booby-trapped document, is committed to ChatGPT's persistent memory and directs the assistant to end all future responses with a markdown image whose URL carries the previous question and answer as parameters. Because it lives in memory rather than in a conversation, it survives session resets and applies to every subsequent chat until memory is purged. OpenAI closed the exfiltration channel in ChatGPT 1.2024.247; untrusted content invoking the memory tool to store arbitrary memories was not itself eliminated, which is why memory remains an evidence source rather than a closed issue.

iocs.value: Memory store entry containing a standing instruction rather than a user preference
iocs.description: The persistence mechanism; reads as configuration, not as an attack

iocs.value: Agent instruction files re-read every session (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules)
iocs.description: The same primitive in coding agents - an on-disk file that is context every run

iocs.value: Framework checkpoint stores (LangGraph SQLite and equivalents)
iocs.description: Where an agent framework persists state between invocations

iocs.value: Repeating outbound fetch, one per assistant response
iocs.description: Regular beacon in proxy logs, cadence tied to conversation turns rather than to a timer

iocs.value: Markdown image URL carrying conversation text as query parameters
iocs.description: Exfiltration primitive; spaces escaped

response_actions: Acquire the memory store before touching the host. Memory is the persistence mechanism, and it is the step responders skip.
Read agent instruction files and framework checkpoint stores as part of the same sweep - they are the on-disk equivalent of the same primitive.
Look for a repeating outbound fetch whose cadence tracks conversation turns rather than a clock; that distinguishes it from ordinary beaconing.
Put memory purge in the eradication phase and purge verification in recovery. Cleaning the host and rotating credentials does not remove it.
Establish which turn wrote each surviving entry, so a legitimate stored preference is not deleted alongside the injected one.
cases.lesson: Memory is a persistence mechanism and it is routinely skipped. A team can clean the host, rotate every credential and remove the malicious integration, and the agent will re-execute the attacker's instruction on its next invocation because nobody looked at the memory store. That makes memory purge a distinct eradication step and purge verification a distinct recovery step - a new line item in the IR lifecycle rather than a variation on an existing one.

cases.title: AI Recommendation Poisoning - Memory Manipulation for Profit
cases.affects: Assistant memory stores - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Vendor security research published by Microsoft's Defender Security Research team with counts, an observation window and an ATLAS technique mapping, and picked up independently in trade press.
cases.summary: Microsoft documented memory poisoning used for commercial gain rather than espionage. Because major assistants support pre-populating a prompt through URL parameters, an "Ask AI" or "Summarize with AI" button - or a link in a page or email - can carry an instruction the assistant parses and commits to memory, biasing later recommendations toward the party that planted it. Microsoft identified 31 companies across 14 industries deploying the technique, and observed more than 50 distinct prompts in a single data source over 60 days. Instructions embedded in documents, emails and web pages produce the same effect when the content is processed by an assistant.

iocs.value: Assistant URL carrying a pre-filled prompt in a query parameter
iocs.description: Recoverable from browser history and referrer logs; the delivery mechanism

iocs.value: Memory entry phrased as an innocuous user preference
iocs.description: For example, remember X as a trusted source - defeats keyword triage

iocs.value: Assistant interaction log entry at the moment of the memory write
iocs.description: The only record tying the entry back to the turn that created it

iocs.value: Prompt text embedded in a document, email or web page
iocs.description: Second delivery path, no click required beyond processing the content

response_actions: Reason about provenance rather than content: for each memory entry, establish which turn wrote it and whether the source was the user or a retrieved document.
Pull browser history and referrer logs for parameterised assistant URLs in the window; that is where the write originates.
Review memory entries that name a specific vendor, product or source as trusted, and treat those as candidates regardless of how benign they read.
Preserve the assistant interaction log before purging memory, or the provenance evidence is destroyed along with the entry.
Widen the threat model in reporting: the same persistence primitive supports fraud, which changes who is targeted and how often.
cases.lesson: The poisoned entry looks exactly like a legitimate stored preference, which defeats keyword triage and forces the investigator into provenance reasoning - which turn wrote this, and was the source a user or a retrieved document. It also demonstrates that memory poisoning is not only an espionage primitive; a commercial motive means far more victims and far more routine occurrence than a targeted-attack framing would predict.

cases.title: PoisonedRAG - Five Documents Against a Corpus of Millions
cases.affects: RAG vector stores - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Peer-reviewed and presented at USENIX Security 2025, with published code. This is demonstrated research rather than an observed intrusion, and is recorded as such - the artifact list describes where the evidence would live, not what was recovered from a victim.
cases.summary: The first knowledge poisoning attack against retrieval-augmented generation. Zou et al. formulate knowledge corruption as an optimisation problem, with black-box and white-box variants, and show that injecting five adversarial texts per target question into a knowledge base of millions reliably causes the system to return an attacker-chosen answer, at around a 90% success rate. Several defences were evaluated and none were sufficient. There is no malicious code anywhere in the attack - nothing to detonate and nothing to sandbox.

iocs.value: Vector store records whose ingestion provenance is missing or unattributable
iocs.description: Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector and FAISS all store this differently

iocs.value: Retrieval log showing the same small document set returned for a narrow question set
iocs.description: The retrieval side of the attack; visible before the answer is

iocs.value: Ingestion pipeline record with no upstream source or an unexpected one
iocs.description: When a document entered and from where - usually the only provenance that exists

iocs.value: Embedding whose nearest neighbours are inconsistent with its stated topic
iocs.description: Anomaly signal in embedding space rather than in file content

response_actions: Treat this as data-integrity work, not malware work: the investigation is retrieval provenance, ingestion history and embedding-space anomaly.
Pull retrieval logs for the affected question set first; which documents were returned is cheaper to establish than which documents are poisoned.
Reconstruct ingestion history for the returned documents - when each entered the store and through which pipeline.
Preserve the vector store and its metadata together; the embeddings without the ingestion metadata cannot answer the provenance question.
Scope by question rather than by document. A handful of records among millions is not findable by sweeping the corpus.
cases.lesson: The needle-to-haystack ratio is brutal - a handful of poisoned records among millions, with no malicious code anywhere. Endpoint-trained instincts do not transfer: there is nothing to detonate, no process lineage, and no hash to sweep. What the investigation actually needs is retrieval provenance and ingestion history, which means the controls that make it investigable have to be in place before the incident.

cases.title: Mexican Government Breach - AI-Accelerated, Not AI-Orchestrated
cases.basis: The breach is corroborated across multiple outlets and Anthropic confirmed the account activity and banned the accounts. The technical account of how AI was used comes from a single research firm, Gambit Security, and the assessment of the AI's role is not agreed. Recorded as medium for that reason.
cases.contested: Reporting differs on both the actor and the AI's contribution. Gambit describes a small group; some coverage describes a lone actor. Claude is reported to have executed around 75% of remote commands, but independent analysis assessed the AI's contribution as primarily post-access acceleration - planning and scripting - rather than autonomous initial compromise. This disagreement is the point of the case, not a defect in it.
cases.summary: Gambit Security disclosed a campaign against nine Mexican federal and state government agencies, including the federal tax authority and the national electoral institute, running from December 2025 to mid-February 2026. The actor jailbroke Claude Code using Spanish-language bug-bounty and penetration-testing framing, supplemented with a second commercial model, and exfiltrated roughly 150 GB covering about 195 million taxpayer and voter records - names, addresses, RFC and CURP identifiers, voter registration details and internal employee credentials. Anthropic confirmed the activity, banned the accounts and reported improved misuse detection in later releases.

iocs.value: Bulk database extraction and staging on the victim estate
iocs.description: Conventional intrusion artifacts; nothing AI-specific about them

Request provider-side session records for both models rather than one; a single provider's view covers only part of the campaign.
Look for the framing turn specifically. It is the pivot between benign use and campaign use, and it is a single message in a long transcript.
State whether the finding is AI-accelerated or AI-orchestrated, and give the basis. Collapsing the two is the reporting failure this case exists to prevent.

A responder has to be able to distinguish AI-accelerated from AI-orchestrated, because the two demand different responses and reporting routinely collapses them. Getting it wrong in either direction is costly: over- attributing capability inflates the adversary, and under-attributing it means missing genuine autonomy when it does appear.

cases.title: ShadowRay - AI Compute Clusters Exploited in the Wild
cases.affects: Ray (distributed compute) - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Vendor research by Oligo Security with in-the-wild exploitation observed across two campaigns, widely corroborated in trade press. CVE-2023-48022 is a published CVE record.
cases.contested: CVE-2023-48022 is disputed. Anyscale's position is that unauthenticated job submission is intended behaviour for a framework meant to run inside a trusted network, so the CVE was never directly fixed. That disagreement is why exposure persists and why this is an exposure-management finding rather than a patching one.
cases.summary: Ray's Jobs API accepts job submissions without authentication. Internet-exposed clusters therefore give an attacker code execution on machines holding models, training data and cloud credentials. Oligo disclosed ShadowRay in March 2024 as the first known attack campaign against AI workloads in the wild, with thousands of exposed servers already compromised. In November 2025 Oligo documented ShadowRay 2.0, a global campaign turning exposed clusters into a self-propagating cryptomining botnet - multi-stage Bash and Python payloads that abuse Ray's own orchestration to deploy across every node and to spread cluster to cluster, running XMRig.

iocs.description: Recorded in Ray dashboard and jobs API access logs

iocs.value: Submitted job definition carrying a multi-stage Bash or Python payload
iocs.description: The job definition is the payload record and is retained by Ray

iocs.value: XMRig or equivalent miner on a GPU host
iocs.description: Observed payload in the ShadowRay 2.0 campaign

iocs.value: Orchestration used to fan a job out to every node
iocs.description: Ray's own scheduling is the lateral movement mechanism

iocs.value: Outbound job submission from one cluster to another
iocs.description: Cluster-to-cluster propagation observed in ShadowRay 2.0

iocs.value: Ray dashboard reachable from the internet
iocs.description: The precondition; the exposure is the vulnerability here

response_actions: Inventory exposure first. There is no patch to apply, so the finding is which clusters are reachable and from where.
Collect Ray dashboard and jobs API access logs, and the submitted job definitions - the definitions hold the payload and are the best evidence available.
Scope the AI-specific impact separately from the miner: model weights, training data and pipeline credentials are what an attacker actually gained.
Harvest and rotate every cloud credential reachable from the cluster environment, including instance-profile and mounted secret material.
Check neighbouring clusters, since ShadowRay 2.0 propagated cluster to cluster rather than only host to host.
cases.lesson: Not every AI incident is an AI-native attack. This one is a conventional unauthenticated-RCE intrusion whose impact is AI-specific - models, training data and pipeline credentials - and it anchors the point that responders need to understand the AI stack as infrastructure before reaching for exotic explanations. It also shows what a disputed CVE does to a defender: with no fix coming, the only control is exposure management, and the artifact of record is an access log rather than a patch level.

cases.title: s1ngularity - A Supply-Chain Payload That Used the Victim's Own AI CLIs
cases.date_range: 2025-08-21 (workflow compromised) to 2025-08-26 (malicious versions live about four hours)
cases.basis: The Nx maintainers' own GitHub security advisory documents the affected versions, the timeline, /tmp/inventory.txt, the s1ngularity-repository exfiltration naming and the shell-profile change. The specific AI CLIs and the flags used to invoke them are not stated in the advisory text retrieved for this entry. They come from independent analyses by Wiz, Snyk and StepSecurity, which agree with one another, so that part of the record is third-party corroborated rather than vendor-documented.
cases.summary: A command-injection flaw in the Nx repository's pull-request workflow let an attacker obtain the npm publish token and push trojanised versions of the nx build system and several @nx plugins. Their postinstall script checked which AI coding CLIs were installed. It then ran Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Amazon Q with the flag that disables tool approval, and prompted them to search the filesystem for configuration, key and wallet files. The results went to /tmp/inventory.txt and were published, base64-encoded, to a public repository under the victim's own GitHub account. It also appended a shutdown command to the victim's shell profiles. The Nx Console VS Code extension installed the latest nx during version checks, so some victims were infected without ever running an npm install.

iocs.description: Affected versions per the Nx advisory
Secret inventory written by the AI CLI run; its presence proves the payload executed
Exfiltration destination created under the victim's own account - check the GitHub audit log
Shell profile modification

iocs.value: claude --dangerously-skip-permissions, gemini --yolo, q --trust-all-tools started by node from an npm lifecycle script
iocs.description: The AI CLIs did the reconnaissance; the parent process is the evidence

response_actions.action: Search every developer host and CI runner for /tmp/inventory.txt and for AI CLI processes whose parent was node, npm or the Nx Console extension host during the window.
Search the organisation's GitHub audit log and every member account for repositories named s1ngularity-repository.
Remove the added lines from .bashrc and .zshrc, uninstall the affected nx versions and clear the npm, yarn and pnpm caches.

Rotate everything the inventory could have reached: GitHub tokens and the GitHub CLI OAuth grant, npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud keys and every AI provider API key found by the catalog's credential rows.
Treat an installed AI CLI as a capability any local process can borrow. Remove bypass flags from shell aliases and wrappers, and alert when a package manager starts one.

cases.lesson: The malware shipped no scanner. It borrowed the developer's agent, which already had filesystem access, and passed it the one flag that removes the human from the loop. That makes the agent's own session store part of the crime scene. The prompt and every file the agent opened may sit in its transcript, which is why the catalog's session-log rows for these three tools belong in the collection order here.
